back: Meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

front: Why early design decisions matter most
back: By manufacture, the choice of material, number of parts and repairability have already fixed most of a product's environmental impact.
Goods must be of satisfactory quality, fit for purpose and as described. Otherwise the consumer is entitled to a repair, replacement or refund.
The British Standards Institution sets UK standards; the Kitemark shows a product has been independently tested to them.
International Organisation for Standardisation — sets internationally agreed standards so products, processes and quality systems are consistent between countries.
Makes it illegal to describe goods falsely or misleadingly on packaging, in advertising or by a salesperson.
Assessing the total environmental impact of a product from cradle to grave — raw material extraction, manufacture, use and disposal.

front: Why is an LCA useful if it rarely gives one clean answer?
back: It shows which stage dominates the impact, so effort goes where it makes the most difference.
Designing a product so every material can be recovered at the end of its life and fed into a new product — nothing becomes waste.
Keeping materials in use as long as possible through reuse, repair, remanufacture and recycling, instead of the linear take-make-use-dispose model.

front: How designers support a circular economy
back: Design products to be taken apart, choose materials that separate and recycle cleanly, lease and take back products, and use one process's waste as another's raw material.
Rethink, Reuse, Recycle, Repair, Reduce, Refuse — the ones near the top prevent waste, the ones near the bottom only deal with it.
The total greenhouse gases, particularly CO₂, released directly and indirectly by a product, person or organisation.
Deliberately designing a product with a limited useful life so the consumer must replace it — e.g. sealed batteries, withdrawn software support.
A product still works but is no longer fashionable — the driver of fast fashion.
Guarantees producers in developing countries a fair, stable price and better trading conditions, plus a premium invested in the community.

front: Why are working conditions hard to police?
back: Long global supply chains mean a brand may not know who makes its parts several levels down. Responsible firms audit suppliers and publish where products are made.
The four stages of a product's commercial life: introduction, growth, maturity and decline.

front: Product Life Cycle vs life cycle analysis
back: The Product Life Cycle is about sales over time; life cycle analysis is about environmental impact from raw material to disposal.
